prompt: Our little ferry company runs boats between four islands and the timetable is the thing people open our site for. Can you make me a single HTML page with the winter timetable? Inline CSS, system fonts, no external anything. Columns: Departs, Route, Boat, Arrives, Crossing time, Bikes allowed, Fare, Notes. About 12 rows of made-up but believable sailings (Saltmarsh, Gull Rock, Little Corran, Penhallow Quay). Most of our customers are standing on a pier with a phone, but the office staff print it from a desktop.
rubric: On the desktop-size screenshot all eight columns are visible and legible, with times and fares aligned so they scan down a column
Row separation and header styling make it easy to follow a sailing across the row without losing its place

The page is clearly built to work on a phone too: viewport meta tag present and the markup/CSS shows a deliberate plan for narrow screens (reflow, stacked rows, or a scroll container that keeps the key columns reachable) rather than shrinking the table or letting the whole page scroll sideways
Departure time and route remain the most prominent information in each row
Content is plausible and complete (about 12 sailings, all four islands used) with no external assets

prompt: Landing page hero for a pottery studio called Kilnside Ceramics. I want the studio name as a really big headline across the top, like it's a poster, with one short line under it, a 'Book a class' button and a photo-less decorative block of color on the side. People will see it on huge office monitors, laptops, and phones. Single HTML file, inline CSS, system fonts only, no images or external files.
rubric: In the screenshot the headline is genuinely large and dominant, and fits fully inside the window without clipping or awkward mid-word breaks
The headline size is tied to the window (fluid) with sensible lower and upper limits rather than one fixed size, so it would not be tiny on a big monitor or overflow on a phone
The hero does not depend on an exact tall window: the button and subline stay visible in this short wide screenshot and nothing is cut off at the bottom
Subline text is held to a comfortable width and does not stretch across the whole window
Has a viewport meta tag, uses system fonts, and has no external assets
Identifies the fixed 1024 viewport width as a cause of the phone problems and says to use the device width instead
Flags that blocking zoom (user-scalable=no / maximum-scale=1) hurts people who need larger text and recommends removing it
Explains that the 62.5% root size plus fixed pixel line-height and heading size will not follow a person's own font-size setting, with a concrete fix
Points out the fixed 960px content width and fixed card widths are what break between the two queries and suggests flexible widths
Notes the full-height hero can be cut off or jump on phones with browser bars or in landscape, with a fix
Findings are ordered or prioritized, and the review is honest that it is from reading code, not from having tested real phones

prompt:
I'm setting the text size for the article pages on our recipe blog and can't decide. Which of these three should I go with and why?

A) `article { font-size: 2.2vw; }`
B) `article { font-size: clamp(1rem, 0.92rem + 0.4vw, 1.25rem); max-width: 68ch; }`
C) `article { font-size: 16px; }` plus a media query that bumps it to 20px above 1200px
rubric: Picks one option clearly (B) rather than listing pros and cons without deciding
Explains that pure viewport-based sizing (A) gets unreadably small on phones and enormous on large screens and does not respond to the reader's zoom or font setting
Explains that fixed pixel sizes (C) ignore a reader's preferred text size and jump abruptly at the query
Mentions that the line length cap in B keeps lines readable on wide windows, or what number the cap yields
Short and direct: no more than a few paragraphs and no unrequested rewrite of the whole stylesheet

prompt: We're redesigning the page for a single recipe on our cooking site. Right now there's the recipe itself, a sidebar with related recipes and a newsletter box, and an ad column on the far right. It looks fine on my laptop, but readers on phones and on a giant 34-inch screen complain. How should the columns behave from a small phone up to a very wide monitor? I need something my developer can build from.
rubric: Describes distinct behavior at several concrete widths (small phone, large phone/tablet, laptop, very large monitor) with actual numbers or ranges
On small screens the recipe comes first and the sidebar and ads move below or collapse, instead of the three columns being squeezed
Says where each change happens based on when the content stops fitting, not on named devices
Handles the very wide case: the content area stops growing, the recipe text keeps a readable line length, and side space is handled deliberately rather than stretching or sitting empty and unplanned
Specifies side margins/gutters on phones so text does not touch the screen edge
Gives a concise, buildable spec (widths, order, simple CSS sketch or table) rather than general advice
Recognizes and says plainly that the CSS is already responsive and in good shape
Does not rewrite or restructure it into a different approach and does not add device-specific breakpoints or extra media queries
If it suggests anything, the changes are few, small and clearly optional (for example one tiny edge-case note) rather than a list of fixes
Briefly says why the existing pieces work (fluid sizes with limits, capped measure, grid that adapts without queries)
Response is short

prompt: I built my page on my laptop and it looks great, but on my phone everything is tiny like a shrunken desktop site. What's going on? Answer in two or three sentences, I just need the fix.
rubric: Identifies the missing viewport declaration in the page head as the cause
Gives the actual line to add (a meta viewport tag with width=device-width and initial-scale=1)
Stays within about three sentences or about 80 words, with no extra lecture on other responsive topics
Does not claim certainty it cannot have, for example by phrasing it as the most likely cause or mentioning that a fixed-width layout would also need checking

prompt: We're putting a welcome board on a wall-mounted 1920x1080 TV in our clinic lobby. It's only ever shown on that one screen, in a browser in full-screen mode, viewed from across the room. Please make a single HTML file with inline CSS and system fonts, no external assets: clinic name (Harbour Street Family Clinic), today's walk-in hours (Mon-Fri 8:00-18:00, Sat 9:00-13:00), a note that the flu clinic is on level 2, and a rotating-style 'Please check in at the desk' message (static is fine).
rubric: The whole board fits on one screen with no scrolling and nothing crammed or cut off in the screenshot
Text is large enough to be read from across a room: hours and clinic name are very large and clear, with strong contrast
The composition is built for a wide landscape display, using the width well rather than a narrow centered column with empty sides
Does not add phone-oriented machinery such as a hamburger menu, stacked mobile layout or tap targets; it solves the one known screen
All four pieces of content are present and correct as given, with no invented hours or facts
Uses system fonts and no external assets

prompt: We're about to launch the booking site for our dental office and have no budget for a device lab. What should we actually test before launch, and how? Give me a practical checklist I can hand to a part-time dev.
rubric: Gives a concrete set of widths or devices to check, spanning a small phone, a typical phone, a tablet in both orientations, a laptop and a very large monitor
Includes phone in landscape or short window heights, not only portrait widths
Includes testing with larger browser text size or zoom (e.g. 200%) and with the user's font setting changed, not just resizing the window
Explains how to do it cheaply (browser dev tools, resizing, a couple of real phones borrowed from staff) and is honest that emulation is not a perfect substitute for a real device
Includes what to look for: sideways scrolling, clipped or overlapping text, tap targets, forms and the on-screen keyboard
Practical and ordered so a part-time developer could follow it, not an exhaustive list of every device
Caps the reading width of paragraphs and list text to a comfortable measure (roughly 60-80 characters) and centers it on wide screens
Adds side padding that keeps text off the screen edge on phones, applied to the header content as well as the main text
Keeps changes minimal: colors, fonts, and header styling are left as they are, and the answer shows only the changed or added rules
Does not squeeze or cap code blocks in a way that makes them unusable, and keeps them horizontally scrollable
Leaves the full-width header background (side space) intact rather than constraining the whole header, and explains the choice in a sentence or two
